At 4:17 every morning, the city became honest.

The bars had closed, the bakeries had not yet opened, and even the traffic lights seemed embarrassed to be performing for empty streets. Red. Green. Amber. An endless rehearsal with no audience.

Mara liked this hour because nothing expected an answer from her.

She walked beneath apartment windows darkened by sleep, past parked cars glossed with rain, past the little grocery where oranges slept in blue crates behind a metal grate. In her coat pocket she carried a key that opened no door she knew.

It had arrived three days earlier in a plain white envelope. No stamp, no return address, only her name written in the handwriting of someone trying to imitate her own.

Inside was the key and a note:

**You’ll know the door when you stop looking for it.**

This was exactly the kind of nonsense Mara disliked. It sounded like something printed on a tea bag or spoken by a man who owned too many scarves. She had thrown the note away.

She had kept the key.

Now it clicked against the coins in her pocket as she walked. She had no destination. Perhaps that was the point, though she resented any mystery that presumed to have a point.

Rain gathered on the brim of her hat. Somewhere, a bottle rolled in the gutter with a hollow, patient sound.

At the corner of Bell Street, Mara noticed a narrow alley between a laundromat and a boarded cinema. She had passed it hundreds of times. Tonight—or this morning—it seemed deeper than before.

She entered.

The alley smelled of wet brick and old electricity. At the far end stood a green door.

Mara stopped.

“Of course,” she said aloud.

The door had no handle, only a keyhole. Above it, someone had painted a small white moon.

She took out the key.

There are moments in life when the world divides neatly into before and after. Usually, we recognize them only in retrospect: the missed train, the answered call, the decision to stay five minutes longer. But occasionally the border announces itself. It waits with theatrical stillness.

Mara inserted the key.

It turned.

Behind the door was her childhood kitchen.

Not a resemblance. Not a reconstruction. The kitchen itself, exactly as it had been before the house was sold: yellow curtains, chipped blue tiles, a wooden table scarred by years of hot pans and hurried breakfasts. The clock above the sink showed 4:17.

Her father sat at the table.

He looked forty-two, which was impossible. He wore the green sweater with the frayed cuff. A mug steamed between his hands.

“You took your time,” he said.

Mara did not move. Grief, she discovered, did not arrive as sadness. It arrived as vertigo.

“You’re dead.”

“Yes.”

“That’s not funny.”

“No,” he agreed. “It wasn’t.”

She wanted to embrace him. She wanted to run. She wanted proof, explanation, apology, and another twenty years. Instead she asked, “What is this place?”

Her father looked around the kitchen.

“A room the world forgot to get rid of.”

“That doesn’t mean anything.”

“You always did prefer instructions.”

“I prefer sense.”

“Sense is just mystery after it gets a uniform.”

“That sounds like something printed on a tea bag.”

He smiled, and the smile broke her.

Mara sat opposite him.

For a while neither spoke. The refrigerator hummed. Rain tapped the window, though beyond the glass there was only darkness.

At last she said, “Did you know?”

“That I was going to die?”

She nodded.

“No. People rarely know the important things in time.”

“I should have visited.”

“Yes.”

The answer struck harder than forgiveness would have.

“I was angry.”

“I know.”

“You never called.”

“I was proud.”

“You could have called.”

“So could you.”

She looked down at the table. One of its scratches curved like a river on a map.

“I’m sorry,” she whispered.

Her father reached across and placed his hand over hers. It felt warm, solid, ordinary.

“I know,” he said.

The clock ticked to 4:18.

The kitchen shuddered.

“What happens now?” Mara asked.

“Now you leave.”

“Can I come back?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because then you’d live here.”

The green door stood open behind her. Beyond it, the alley waited in the rain.

She clung to his hand.

“I don’t want to forget you.”

“You will,” he said gently. “In pieces. Then you’ll remember me in pieces. That’s how it works.”

The walls began to fade. First the yellow curtains, then the blue tiles, then the old refrigerator and its familiar hum.

Her father remained.

“Wait,” Mara said. “There’s so much I need to tell you.”

“There always is.”

“What should I do?”

He looked at her with infinite fondness and a trace of impatience.

“Something that isn’t waiting.”

Then he was gone.

Mara stood alone in the alley. The green door had vanished. In her palm lay the key, now soft with rust.

At the end of the street, the traffic lights continued their lonely sequence. Red. Green. Amber.

A bakery switched on its windows.

The sky began, almost reluctantly, to brighten.

Mara walked toward the smell of bread.
